1.title: What C Is and Why
1.theory:
## What C is

C — a low-level compiled language. Created in 1972 at Bell Labs (Dennis Ritchie) for Unix. Used in: operating systems (Linux, parts of Windows), embedded systems, drivers, databases (PostgreSQL, SQLite), compilers, high-load servers.

## Why learn C

- Foundation for C++, C#, Objective-C, Go, Rust.
- You understand memory, pointers, how things work "under the hood".
- Small language — learns quickly.
- Fast and predictable.

## How it differs from Python and Java

- **No garbage collector** — you free memory yourself.
- **Pointers** — direct memory access.
- **No classes** — only `struct`.
- **Compiles to machine code** (not bytecode like Java).
- **No automatic checks** — easy to shoot yourself in the foot.

## Compiled, not interpreted

Python reads and executes line by line. C first **compiles** to machine code, then runs. The program is a separate `.exe`/`.out` file.

## What C does NOT have

- Strings are not objects — they are `char[]`.
- No exceptions.
- No `try/catch`.
- No built-in collections (lists, dicts) — write them or use libraries.
- No automatic memory management.

## Standards

C89, C99, C11, C17, C23. In this course — C11 (modern and widespread).

## Summary

- C is low-level, compiled
- Foundation for many languages
- Pointers, manual memory
- No OOP, no exceptions
- Fast, predictable

2.title: Compilation: gcc
2.theory:
## How C becomes a program

`.c` file → compiler → `.o` (object) → linker → executable. Usually one `gcc` command does everything.

## gcc

**GCC** — GNU Compiler Collection. For C — `gcc`, for C++ — `g++`.

```bash
gcc hello.c -o hello
./hello
```

- `-o hello` — output filename
- Without `-o` — `a.out` (Linux/macOS) or `a.exe` (Windows MinGW)

## Simple example

`hello.c`:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello\n");
    return 0;
}
```

Compile:
```bash
gcc hello.c -o hello
./hello
```

## Flags

- `-Wall -Wextra` — warnings
- `-std=c11` — standard
- `-g` — debug info (for gdb)
- `-O2` — optimization

Usually: `gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c11 hello.c -o hello`.

## Errors

- **Compile error** — syntax, types. Program won't be created.
- **Link error** — function not found (`undefined reference`).
- **Runtime error** — segfault, division by zero.

## Windows

Via MinGW (`gcc` in PATH) or WSL. In Visual Studio — `cl.exe`, syntax is the same.

## What if

- Forget `-o` — file will be `a.out`.
- Forget `#include` — function not declared.
- Typo in filename — `file not found`.

## Summary

- `gcc file.c -o name`
- `-Wall -Wextra` — warnings
- `-std=c11` — standard
- Errors: compile / link / runtime

3.title: First Program
3.theory:
## Minimal program

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello, world!\n");
    return 0;
}
```

## Breakdown

- `#include <stdio.h>` — include standard I/O library header. Without it, `printf` is not declared.
- `int main(void)` — entry point. `int` — return code, `void` — no parameters.
- `{ ... }` — function body.
- `printf("...\n")` — output. `\n` — newline.
- `return 0;` — successful exit. Non-zero — error.

## `#include`

```c
#include <stdio.h>   // system header
#include "my.h"      // own file
```

`<...>` — from system folders. `"..."` — from current directory.

## Difference from Java

- No class, method, `public static void`. Only `int main`.
- No automatic `println`. `printf` doesn't move to a new line — add `\n`.
- `void` in parens — "no parameters".

## Return code

```c
return 0;    // success
return 1;    // error
```

Checked by the system (shell, CI). Forgetting `return 0` in `main` — usually not an error (implicit 0), but **always** write it explicitly.

## Comments

```c
// single line
/*
   multi-line
*/
```

## What if

- Forget `;` — compile error.
- Forget `\n` — next line sticks to previous.
- Forget `return 0;` — not critical, but bad style.

## Summary

- `#include <stdio.h>` — for `printf`
- `int main(void)` — entry point
- `printf("...\n")` — output
- `return 0` — success
- `;` at end of each statement

4.title: int, char, float, double
4.theory:
## Basic types

```c
int age = 25;           // integer
char letter = 'A';      // single character
float price = 99.99f;   // float (~7 digits)
double pi = 3.14159;    // double (~15 digits)
```

## Sizes

- `char` — 1 byte (usually)
- `int` — 4 bytes (usually)
- `float` — 4 bytes
- `double` — 8 bytes

Exact sizes — via `sizeof(int)` etc. On different platforms may vary.

## Suffixes

```c
float f = 3.14f;     // f — mandatory for float
long n = 100000L;    // L — long
unsigned int u = 5u; // u — unsigned
```

Without `f`, literal `3.14` is `double` by default.

## Modifiers

- `short` / `long` — size
- `unsigned` — only positive (larger range)
- `signed` — signed (default)

```c
unsigned int x = 4000000000u;   // fits only like this
short int small = 100;
long long big = 9000000000LL;
```

## char is int

`char` is also a number (ASCII code):

```c
char c = 'A';
printf("%d\n", c);   // 65
```

## Declaration and initialization

```c
int a = 5;     // with initialization
int b;         // NO initialization — garbage
int c = 0;     // explicit zero
```

**Important:** a local variable without initialization contains **garbage**, not 0. Common source of bugs.

## Constants

```c
const int MAX = 100;
// MAX = 200; // compile error
#define SIZE 10
```

`const` — typed. `#define` — preprocessor, textual replacement. Modern code prefers `const`.

## What if

- `float f = 3.14;` without `f` — warning, possible precision loss.
- Use `b` without initialization — garbage.
- `char c = "A"` (double quotes) — error, `"A"` is a string.

## Common mistake

`char c = "A"` instead of `char c = 'A'`. Single quotes — character, double — string.

## Summary

- `int`, `char`, `float`, `double`
- Sizes via `sizeof()`
- Suffixes `f`, `L`
- `char` is also a number
- Local without initialization — garbage
- `const` — constant

5.title: printf: Formatting
5.theory:
## Basic specifiers

```c
printf("%d\n", 42);       // integer
printf("%f\n", 3.14);     // double/float (6 digits)
printf("%c\n", 'A');      // character
printf("%s\n", "hello");  // string
```

## Precision

```c
printf("%.2f\n", 3.14159);   // 3.14
printf("%8.2f\n", 3.14);     // "    3.14" (width 8)
printf("%08.2f\n", 3.14);    // "00003.14" (zeros)
```

Format: `%[width][.precision]type`.

## Multiple arguments

```c
printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", 5, 10);
printf("%s: %d\n", "age", 25);
```

Each `%` takes an argument in order. **Type mismatch** — UB (garbage in output).

## Special

- `%%` — the `%` character
- `%ld` — long
- `%u` — unsigned int
- `%lf` — double in scanf (in printf — `%f`)
- `%x` — hex

## printf in C vs Java

- Java: `System.out.printf("%.2f%n", x)`. C: `printf("%.2f\n", x)`. `\n` not `%n`.
- Java: `%d` for int, C: same.

## What if

- `%d` for `double` — UB, garbage.
- Forget `\n` — lines stick.
- Forget argument — UB.

## Common mistake

`printf("%d\n", 3.14)` — outputs garbage. `%d` expects `int`.

## Summary

- `%d`, `%f`, `%c`, `%s`
- `%.2f` — 2 digits
- `%8.2f` — width 8
- `%%` — `%` symbol
- `\n` — newline
- Type must match

6.title: Type Casting
6.theory:
## Implicit

```c
int a = 10;
double b = a;        // int → double, automatic
int c = 3.99;        // double → int, TRUNCATION, c = 3
```

Automatically: smaller → larger (safe). Larger → smaller — precision loss.

## Explicit

```c
double d = 3.99;
int i = (int) d;     // 3
int j = (int) 10.0 / 4;  // 10 / 4 = 2
```

`(int)` — C-style cast. In C++ prefer `static_cast<int>(d)`.

## Integer division

```c
int a = 7, b = 2;
int c = a / b;                // 3, not 3.5!
double d = (double) a / b;    // 3.5
double e = a / (double) b;    // 3.5
```

`int / int = int`. Want a fraction — cast **one** operand.

## char → int

```c
char c = 'A';
int code = c;         // 65
char d = 65;          // 'A'
```

## Dangerous casts

```c
int big = 1000000000;
short small = (short) big;    // overflow, garbage
double d = 3.99;
int i = (int) d;              // 3 — truncation, not rounding
```

## sizeof and casting

`sizeof(int)` returns `size_t` (unsigned). Comparison `sizeof(int) > -1` is false due to conversion.

## What if

- `int` to `double` — ok.
- `double` to `int` without cast — warning.
- `(int) 3.99` — 3, not 4 (truncation).
- `(short) big` when large — garbage.

## Common mistake

`7 / 2` gives `3`, not `3.5`. Cast: `(double) 7 / 2`.

## Summary

- `int / int = int` — fractional part truncated
- `(double) x` — explicit
- `(int) 3.99` = 3
- Overflow → garbage
- `char` ↔ `int` — ASCII code

7.title: const and Sizes
7.theory:
## const

```c
const int MAX = 100;
// MAX = 200; // compile error

const double PI = 3.14159;
```

`const` — **typed** constant. Checked by the compiler.

## #define

```c
#define SIZE 10
int arr[SIZE];  // preprocessor substitutes 10
```

`#define` — textual replacement. **No type**, no checks. Modern code prefers `const`.

## Difference

```c
const int A = 10;    // compiler checks
#define B 10        // just text

// A = 20;  // error
// B = 20;  // preprocessor substitutes `10 = 20` — syntax error
```

## sizeof

```c
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(int));     // 4 (usually)
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(char));    // 1
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(double));  // 8
```

`%zu` — format for `size_t`.

## Array size

```c
int arr[10];
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]));  // 10
```

`sizeof(arr)` — entire array in bytes. Divide by element size — number of elements.

## sizeof and pointer

```c
int arr[10];
int *p = arr;
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(arr));  // 40
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(p));    // 8 (pointer size)
```

For a pointer, `sizeof` returns the **pointer** size, not the array.

## What if

- `const` without initialization — error.
- `sizeof` from pointer instead of array — wrong result.
- `#define` with complex expression without parens — trap.

## Common mistake

`sizeof(arr)` in a function where `arr` is a parameter. Parameter is a pointer, `sizeof` returns pointer size, not array size.

## Summary

- `const` — typed constant
- `#define` — textual
- `sizeof(type)` — size
- `sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0])` — length
- For pointer — pointer size

8.title: scanf: Reading
8.theory:
## What scanf is

`scanf` reads user input. Analog of `input()` in Python, `Scanner` in Java.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int x;
    scanf("%d", &x);
    printf("You entered: %d\n", x);
    return 0;
}
```

## Ampersand `&`

`scanf("%d", &x)` — **address** of the variable. `scanf` knows where to put the value. Without `&` — UB (crashes).

**Exception:** `scanf("%s", str)` — strings are already an address (array). No `&`.

## Specifiers

```c
int n;
scanf("%d", &n);

double d;
scanf("%lf", &d);   // for double — %lf

char c;
scanf(" %c", &c);   // space before %c — skip whitespace

char s[100];
scanf("%s", s);     // no & — s is already an address
```

## `%lf` for double

In `printf` — `%f`. In `scanf` — **`%lf`** for `double`. `%f` for `float`.

## `%s` and spaces

`%s` reads up to whitespace. Input "Ivan Petrov" with `%s` gives only "Ivan".

## What if

- Forget `&` — UB, program crashes or garbage.
- `%d` for `double` — garbage.
- `%s` for strings without size — buffer overflow (dangerous).

## Common mistake

`scanf("%d", x)` without `&`. Need `scanf("%d", &x)`.

## Summary

- `scanf("%d", &x)` — integer
- `scanf("%lf", &d)` — double
- `scanf("%s", str)` — string, no `&`
- `&` — address for numbers
- `%s` — up to whitespace
- No `&` for numbers — UB

10.title: if / else, Ternary
10.theory:
## Syntax

```c
if (x > 0) {
    printf("positive\n");
} else if (x < 0) {
    printf("negative\n");
} else {
    printf("zero\n");
}
```

Condition in parens, body in braces.

## Operators

`==` `!=` `<` `>` `<=` `>=`. `=` is assignment, not comparison.

```c
if (x = 5) { }    // ERROR: assignment! x becomes 5, condition always true
if (x == 5) { }   // correct
```

The `-Wall` compiler warns. But better not to make the mistake.

## Logical

```c
if (age >= 18 && has_passport) { }
if (name == 'A' || name == 'B') { }
if (!ok) { }
```

`&&` — and, `||` — or, `!` — not.

## Ternary

```c
int x = 5;
const char *s = x > 0 ? "positive" : "negative";
printf("%s\n", s);
```

`condition ? if_true : if_false`.

## Truth and falsity

C has **no** `bool` type in older versions. With `#include <stdbool.h>`, `true`/`false` exist. Without it:
- `0` — false
- **anything else** — true (`1`, `-1`, `"abc"` etc.)

```c
if (5) { }    // true
if (0) { }    // false
```

## What if

- `if (x = 5)` — assignment, condition always true.
- Forget braces for two statements — only the first is in the `if`.
- `int x = 5 > 3;` — `x = 1` (true).

## Common mistake

`if (x = 5)` instead of `if (x == 5)`. Always compile with `-Wall`.

## Summary

- `if (condition) { }` — parens and braces
- `else if`, `else`
- `&&`, `||`, `!`
- `a ? b : c` — ternary
- `0` — false, anything else — true
- `=` vs `==` — different

12.title: Logical Operators
12.theory:
## Basics

```c
if (a > 0 && b > 0) { }   // and
if (a == 0 || b == 0) { }  // or
if (!flag) { }             // not
```

## Tables

`&&`:
| A | B | A && B |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | F |

`||`:
| A | B | A \|\| B |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | T |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | F |

## Short-circuit

`&&` and `||` **do not evaluate** the second operand if the result is already clear:

```c
if (b != 0 && a / b > 2) { }
```

If `b == 0`, `a / b` is **not evaluated** — no division by zero.

Useful for checks:

```c
if (ptr != NULL && ptr->value > 0) { }
```

Without `&&` — segfault.

## Result

`&&` and `||` in C return **0 or 1**, not the operands themselves (unlike Python).

```c
int x = 5 && 10;   // x = 1
int y = 0 || 42;   // y = 1
```

## Precedence

`!` > `&&` > `||`. Unsure — use parens.

## What if

- `a == 1 || 2` — always true, because `2` is true.
- `x && y` without parens with several — precedence confuses.

## Common mistake

`if (x == 1 || 2)` — wanted "x is 1 or 2", got "x is 1 OR true" — always true. Correct: `if (x == 1 || x == 2)`.

## Summary

- `&&` — and, `||` — or, `!` — not
- Short-circuit — second operand may not be evaluated
- Result — 0 or 1
- Precedence: `!` > `&&` > `||`
- `x == 1 || 2` — mistake

options: Second operand not evaluated if result is clear

13.title: for
13.theory:
## Syntax

```c
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    printf("%d\n", i);
}
```

Three parts via `;`: **initialization**; **condition**; **step**.

## Step by step

1. `int i = 0` — once.
2. `i < 5` — check before each iteration.
3. Body.
4. `i++` — after the body.
5. Repeat from step 2.

## Reverse

```c
for (int i = 5; i > 0; i--) {
    printf("%d\n", i);  // 5, 4, 3, 2, 1
}
```

## Step

```c
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i += 2) {
    printf("%d\n", i);  // 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
}
```

## Declaration outside

```c
int i;
for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) { }
printf("%d\n", i);  // 5 — i visible after the loop
```

With `int i` **inside** — `i` lives only in the loop (C99+).

## Infinite

```c
for (;;) { }   // equivalent to while (1)
```

## What if

- Forget `i++` — infinite loop.
- `i <= 5` instead of `< 5` — one extra iteration.
- Use `i` outside loop (C99) — error.

## Common mistake

`for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++)` — goes through 0..5 (6 times), not 0..4.

## Summary

- `for (init; cond; step)` — three parts
- `int i` inside — loop-only
- `for (;;)` — infinite
- Don't forget the step

17.title: void, Prototypes
17.theory:
## void

`void` — "nothing". Two uses:

### 1. As return type

```c
void greet(void) {
    printf("Hi\n");
}
```

Function returns nothing. `return;` (no value) — just exit.

### 2. As parameter

```c
int main(void) {
    // no parameters
}
```

`(void)` = "no parameters". Old style, but idiomatic.

## Function prototype

Declaration **before** use, without body:

```c
int sum(int a, int b);  // prototype

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", sum(2, 3));
    return 0;
}

int sum(int a, int b) {  // definition
    return a + b;
}
```

The compiler knows the signature at the call site. Works.

## Why prototype

- Split code: header `foo.h` + implementation `foo.c`.
- Mutual recursion.
- Order in the file doesn't matter.

## Without prototype

If `main` calls `sum` before its declaration — modern C gives a **warning** or error (`implicit declaration`). In C89 it worked, in C99+ it doesn't.

## Header file

`math_utils.h`:

```c
#ifndef MATH_UTILS_H
#define MATH_UTILS_H

int sum(int a, int b);

#endif
```

`math_utils.c`:

```c
#include "math_utils.h"

int sum(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}
```

## What if

- `void f(void) { return 5; }` — error.
- Call without a prototype — compile error in C99+.
- `void` as a normal variable — error.

## Common mistake

`void main()` — **not** standard. Correct is `int main(void) { ... return 0; }`.

## Summary

- `void` — no return / no parameters
- `int main(void)` — standard
- Prototype: `int sum(int, int);`
- Definition — with body
- `void main()` — legacy

19.title: Arrays: Creation, Indices
19.theory:
## Array

```c
int arr[5];              // 5 elements, garbage
int nums[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};   // 5, from literal
int zeros[10] = {0};     // all zeros
```

Length **fixed** at creation.

## Indices

From zero. `arr[0]` — first, `arr[4]` — fifth. `arr[5]` — **out of bounds**, UB (may crash, may not).

## Length

```c
int arr[5];
int n = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]);  // 5
```

**Only** for arrays, not pointers. In a function parameter `int arr[]` — pointer, `sizeof` returns pointer size.

## Assignment

```c
arr[0] = 10;
arr[1] = 20;
```

## Out of bounds

```c
int arr[3] = {1, 2, 3};
arr[5] = 100;    // UB — overwrites another memory
```

Doesn't crash immediately — may corrupt another variable. Classic bug.

## Initialization

```c
int a[5] = {1, 2, 3};    // {1, 2, 3, 0, 0} — rest are 0
int b[5] = {0};          // all zeros
int c[] = {1, 2, 3};     // length 3
```

## What if

- `arr[10]` for length 5 — UB.
- Array without initialization — garbage.
- `sizeof(arr)` in a function — pointer size.

## Common mistake

Out of bounds is **not checked** in C. Program may run with a bug that manifests later.

## Summary

- `int arr[5]` — fixed length
- Indices 0..4
- `sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0])` — length
- Out of bounds — UB
- `{0}` — all zeros

21.title: Strings: char[], Null Terminator
21.theory:
## String in C

Strings in C are **`char` arrays** ending with a **null** `'\0'`:

```c
char str[6] = "hello";    // 'h','e','l','l','o','\0'
```

`strlen(str)` = 5, but `sizeof(str)` = 6 (with null).

## Creating

```c
char s1[] = "hello";       // length 6 (5 + \0)
char s2[6] = "hello";     // exactly fits
char s3[10] = "hi";       // 'h','i',0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0
char s4[] = {'h', 'i', '\0'};  // same
```

## Without null — not a string

```c
char s[] = {'h', 'i'};   // array of 2 char, NOT a string (no \0)
printf("%s\n", s);     // UB — printf looks for \0, reads garbage
```

## Input

```c
char name[50];
scanf("%s", name);       // no &, up to whitespace
fgets(name, 50, stdin);  // whole line, including spaces
```

`scanf` without size — **dangerous** (overflow). `fgets` is safe.

## Length

```c
printf("%zu\n", strlen(str));   // without \0
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(str));   // with \0
```

## What if

- Forget `\0` — UB on `printf("%s")`.
- `char s[5] = "hello";` — no room for `\0`, error/garbage.
- `scanf("%s")` with a long string — buffer overflow.

## Common mistake

`char s[5] = "hello";` — not enough room for `\0`. Need at least 6.

## Summary

- String is `char[]` + `'\0'` at the end
- Length = characters + 1
- `scanf("%s")` — up to whitespace, no `&`
- `fgets` — whole line, safe
- `strlen` — without null, `sizeof` — with null

22.title: string.h: strlen, strcpy, strcmp
22.theory:
## strlen

```c
#include <string.h>

size_t len = strlen("hello");   // 5
```

Returns `size_t` (unsigned). Without `\0`.

## strcpy — copy

```c
char dst[20];
strcpy(dst, "hello");
```

Copies up to `\0`. **Does not check** the size of `dst` — overflow if too small.

Safe variant — `strncpy`:

```c
strncpy(dst, "hello", sizeof(dst) - 1);
dst[sizeof(dst) - 1] = '\0';
```

## strcat — concatenation

```c
char s[20] = "Hello";
strcat(s, ", world");    // "Hello, world"
```

Appends at the end. Also does not check size.

## strcmp — comparison

```c
if (strcmp(a, b) == 0) { }   // equal
if (strcmp(a, b) < 0) { }    // a < b
if (strcmp(a, b) > 0) { }    // a > b
```

**Not** `a == b` — that compares **pointers**, not contents.

## strchr, strstr

```c
char *pos = strchr("hello", 'l');      // position of first 'l'
char *sub = strstr("hello world", "world");  // substring position or NULL
```

## What if

- `strcpy` into a small buffer — overflow (UB).
- `if (a == b)` for strings — compares addresses, not contents.
- `strcmp` without `#include <string.h>` — error.

## Common mistake

`if (str1 == str2)` for strings — **never** use. Only `strcmp`.

## Summary

- `strlen` — length
- `strcpy` — copy (dangerous)
- `strcat` — concatenation
- `strcmp` — content comparison
- `strstr` — substring search
- `==` for strings — addresses only

23.title: Pointers: Addresses, &
23.theory:
## What a pointer is

A pointer is a variable that stores the **address** of another variable.

```c
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;    // p stores the address of x
```

- `&x` — address of x
- `*p` — type "pointer to int"

## Syntax

```c
int *p;         // pointer to int
char *s;        // pointer to char (often — a string)
double *d;      // pointer to double
```

`int* p` or `int *p` — same, `*` binds to the variable but not to the type.

## Address in printf

```c
int x = 10;
printf("%p\n", (void*)&x);   // address in hex: 0x7ffe...
```

`%p` — specifier for a pointer.

## Pointer and its value

```c
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;

printf("%p\n", (void*)p);    // address, e.g. 0x7ffe1234
printf("%d\n", *p);          // 10 — value at address
```

`p` — address. `*p` — value at address.

## Why pointers

- Modify a variable from a function.
- Work with dynamic memory (`malloc`).
- Efficiently pass large structs.
- Pointer arithmetic, arrays.

## NULL

```c
int *p = NULL;   // points nowhere
if (p != NULL) { /* safe to dereference */ }
```

Dereferencing `NULL` — segfault.

## What if

- `int *p = 5;` — error (number not an address).
- Dereference `NULL` — segfault.
- Use `%p` with a non-pointer — UB.

## Common mistake

`printf("%d", p)` for a pointer — UB. Need `%p` and cast `(void*)`.

## Summary

- `&x` — address
- `*p` — dereference
- `int *p = &x` — store address
- `%p` — address output
- `NULL` — points nowhere
- Dereferencing NULL — segfault

24.title: Dereference *
24.theory:
## Dereference

`*p` — the value at the address `p` points to.

```c
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;

printf("%d\n", *p);    // 10
*p = 20;                // change x through p
printf("%d\n", x);     // 20
```

## Change through pointer

```c
void increment(int *p) {
    (*p)++;    // parens mandatory: *p++ is different
}

int x = 5;
increment(&x);
printf("%d\n", x);   // 6
```

`(*p)++` — increment the value. `*p++` — move the pointer (not what we want).

## Why pointers in functions

```c
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int t = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = t;
}

int x = 1, y = 2;
swap(&x, &y);
printf("%d %d\n", x, y);   // 2 1
```

Without pointers swap wouldn't work — copies are passed.

## Pointer to pointer

```c
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;
int **pp = &p;
printf("%d\n", **pp);   // 10
```

## Const pointers

```c
const int *p = &x;   // cannot *p = 5
int * const p = &x;  // cannot p = &y
const int * const p = &x;   // neither
```

## What if

- `*p` with `p` not initialized — UB (garbage address, segfault).
- `*p++` instead of `(*p)++` — different operation.
- Dereference NULL — segfault.

## Common mistake

`*p++` is `*(p++)`, pointer shift, not value increment. Need parens `(*p)++`.

## Summary

- `*p` — value at address
- `*p = x` — write
- `(*p)++` — increment value
- For swap — pointers
- `**pp` — pointer to pointer

25.title: malloc / free
25.theory:
## Dynamic memory

Array `int arr[5]` — fixed length. Want flexible — `malloc`.

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

int *arr = malloc(5 * sizeof(int));
if (arr == NULL) {
    // allocation error
    return 1;
}
// use
arr[0] = 10;
free(arr);
```

## malloc

```c
void *malloc(size_t size);
```

Returns `void*` — pointer to block or `NULL`. Doesn't initialize (garbage).

## calloc

```c
int *arr = calloc(5, sizeof(int));   // zeroes
```

`calloc(count, size)`. All bytes 0.

## realloc

```c
arr = realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int));   // grow
```

## free

```c
free(arr);
```

**Mandatory** after `malloc`. Forget — leak.

## Double free — UB

```c
free(arr);
free(arr);    // UB — crash or corruption
```

## Use after free

```c
free(arr);
arr[0] = 10;   // UB
```

The pointer after `free` is invalid. Assign `NULL`:

```c
free(arr);
arr = NULL;
```

## Check

```c
if (arr == NULL) {
    printf("Out of memory\n");
    return 1;
}
```

Always check!

## What if

- Forget `free` — leak.
- `free` twice — UB.
- Use after `free` — UB.
- Don't check `NULL` — segfault.

## Common mistake

Leaks in a loop: `malloc` without `free`.

## Summary

- `malloc(size)` — allocate
- `calloc(n, size)` — allocate with zeroes
- `realloc` — resize
- `free` — free
- Check NULL
- After `free` — `NULL`

26.title: Pointers and Arrays
26.theory:
## Array — pointer to first

```c
int arr[] = {10, 20, 30};
int *p = arr;   // same as &arr[0]
```

Array name — **address of the first element**. Not a full pointer (can't `arr = ...`), but works as one in expressions.

## Indexing and arithmetic

```c
int arr[] = {10, 20, 30};

printf("%d\n", arr[0]);      // 10
printf("%d\n", *(arr + 0));  // 10 — same
printf("%d\n", arr[1]);      // 20
printf("%d\n", *(arr + 1));  // 20
```

`arr[i]` = `*(arr + i)`.

## Pointer arithmetic

`p + 1` — not +1 byte, but +1 **element** (+ `sizeof(int)` bytes).

```c
int *p = arr;
printf("%d\n", *p);       // 10
p++;                      // shift by 1 element
printf("%d\n", *p);       // 20
```

## Traversal

```c
int arr[] = {10, 20, 30};
int *p = arr;
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    printf("%d\n", *(p + i));
}
```

Or via `p++`:

```c
for (int *p = arr; p < arr + 3; p++) {
    printf("%d\n", *p);
}
```

## Array in function

```c
void printArr(int *arr, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%d ", arr[i]);
}

int arr[] = {1, 2, 3};
printArr(arr, 3);
```

`int arr[]` and `int *arr` in parameters — **same**. Size via `sizeof` doesn't work (it's a pointer).

## What if

- `sizeof(arr)` in a function — pointer size.
- `arr = ...` — error (array name not reassigned).
- `p++` beyond array — UB.

## Common mistake

`sizeof(arr)` in a function parameter — gives pointer size, not array. Pass `n` separately.

## Summary

- `arr` — address of the first
- `arr[i]` = `*(arr + i)`
- `p++` — shift by element
- Array in function — pointer
- `sizeof` doesn't work in parameters
